steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Latin verbs are conjugated (change form) to show person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), number (singular, plural), tense (when), voice (active/passive), and mood (indicative/subjunctive).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: There are four conjugations, identified by the characteristic vowel in the present stem: 1st (-a-), 2nd (-e-), 3rd (short -e- or consonant), 4th (-i-).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Every Latin verb has four principal parts that must be memorised: e.g. laudo, laudare, laudavi, laudatus (I praise, to praise, I praised, praised).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What are the four principal parts of a Latin verb? | Q: How do you identify which conjugation a verb belongs to? | Q: What are the present tense personal endings?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: First person singular present active indicative, present infinitive, first person singular perfect active indicative, and perfect passive participle. Example: laudo, laudare, laudavi, laudatus. | By the characteristic vowel in the present infinitive (second principal part): 1st -are (a), 2nd -ere (e), 3rd -ere (short e/consonant), 4th -ire (i). | -o/m (1st singular), -s (2nd singular), -t (3rd singular), -mus (1st plural), -tis (2nd plural), -nt (3rd plural).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always learn all four principal parts of every verb — you cannot form the perfect or passive without them. When translating, identify the verb first: find its person, number, tense, and voice to establish the sentence’s core meaning. Irregular verbs (especially sum and possum) appear frequently in set texts and exams — learn their forms thoroughly. For the perfect tense, learn the stem from the third principal part: drop -i to get the stem (laudavi → laudav-).
